I used to think that computers were reprogrammable hardware devices that could be used for many purposes. I no longer think so. The things that we call "computers" are just glorified calculators that make the act of compute-ing easier through the use of hardware. When you are faced with a non-computing problem, like robotics, you have 2 choices:
- use a glorified calculator and warp the problem until it fits onto a glorified calculator
- invent a new device that suits the problem better.
1. just enough checking to keep design consistent
2. lots of type management to allow compiler to optimize
IMO, FoCers *should* be inventing completely new devices (a la The Mother Of All Demos), but, instead FoCers seem to just push the boundaries of warping problems to fit onto glorified calculators.

CPUs do not directly implement function-based programming. CPUs use subroutines (not functions), use mutation, use control flow, etc. We have to create scaffolding to fake out functions on top of CPUs, much like Prolog programmers need to create scaffolding to fake out relational programming on CPUs. It appears that people have forgotten that compute-ation is not the same as CPU-based hardware. Since Fortran, C, Lisp, Smalltalk, etc., etc. we have been using the function-based scaffolding as a basis for our work and have been forcing all of our problems onto this scaffolding whether suitable or not. Sector Lisp is a glaring example of what the FP paradigm really is. When you stick to the paradigm, you get a lean engine with a lean GC. When you push the paradigm beyond its sweet spot, you get bloat and edicts that cause cognitive dissonance when you think of the hardware (edicts like "no mutation", yet, CPUs are all about mutation).
